- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: ShareOnboardingGuide
tools.description:
Upload the ONBOARDING.md in the current directory and return a share link teammates can open in Claude Code. Call this after the user has confirmed the final content.

When called with the default mode='check': if a local ONBOARDING.md is present, uploads it to the most-recently-updated org guide (or creates one if none exist) and returns a fresh link. If no local file is present, returns the existing link without uploading (status: has_existing).

mode.description: 'check' (default): if ONBOARDING.md is present locally, uploads it to the most-recent guide (creates one if none exist); otherwise reports the existing link without uploading. 'update': upload to a specific guide by short_code. 'create': always make a new link. 'delete': remove the guide named by short_code; with no short_code, nothing is deleted and the user's guides are listed.

short_code.description: Short code of one guide, from an earlier call's result. Required by delete. With check or update, targets that guide instead of the most recently updated one.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Linear__list_comments
tools.description: List comments on a Linear issue, project, initiative, document, project milestone, or project/initiative status update. Provide exactly one of `issueId`, `projectId`, `initiativeId`, `documentId`, `milestoneId`, or `statusUpdateId`. `statusUpdateType` applies only to `statusUpdateId`; omit it for every other parent. For issues, projects, and initiatives this returns both top-level discussion threads and inline description comments. Inline (anchored) comments carry a non-null `quotedText` set to the snippet of description text they reference. Returned comments include `author` and nullable `onBehalfOf`; when set, `onBehalfOf` identifies the user the agent author acted for. Files uploaded in comment bodies are returned in `attachments` with titles and download URLs, not issue attachment IDs. Signed upload URLs expire after five minutes; call list_comments again to refresh them. Download documents using these URLs and process them with your own file tools.

tools.description: Create or update a comment on a Linear issue, project, initiative, document, project milestone, or project/initiative status update. If `id` is provided, updates the existing comment; otherwise creates a new one. To start a new thread, pass `body` and exactly one of `issueId`, `projectId`, `initiativeId`, `documentId`, `milestoneId`, or `statusUpdateId` (`statusUpdateType` applies only to `statusUpdateId`; omit it for every other parent) — comments on issues/projects/initiatives become top-level discussion threads; comments on documents/milestones become description comments. A status update holds a single thread, so a comment on an update that already has one is added to it as a reply. To reply to an existing thread, pass `parentId` and `body`; the reply inherits the parent's thread type, so no entity reference is needed. Parent reference fields are ignored when `id` or `parentId` is provided (`statusUpdateType` is rejected instead).

id.description: Comment ID. If provided, updates the existing comment

issueId.description: Issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). P-prefixed identifiers (e.g., P-ENG-123) are projects, not issues (provide exactly one parent)

projectId.description: Project name, ID, identifier (e.g., P-ENG-123), or slug (provide exactly one parent)

initiativeId.description: Initiative name, ID, identifier (e.g., I-123), or slug (provide exactly one parent)

documentId.description: Document ID or slug (provide exactly one parent)

milestoneId.description: Milestone UUID (provide exactly one parent). Resolve milestone names via `list_milestones` first.

statusUpdateId.description: Status update UUID (provide exactly one parent). Resolve status updates via `get_status_updates` first.

statusUpdateType.description: Set only together with `statusUpdateId`; omit for issue, project, initiative, document, and milestone comments. Type of status update named by `statusUpdateId`, as returned by `get_status_updates`. Omit to check both project and initiative status updates.

parentId.description: Parent comment ID (for replies, only when creating)

body.description: Content as Markdown. Do not escape the string — use literal newlines and special characters, not escape sequences. To mention a user, use @displayName (e.g., @johndoe). To embed an image or file, upload it with prepare_file_upload and insert the returned markdown

content.text:
{"messages":"THREAD: :review: another fix (this time smaller) as follow-up from the openclaw incident <https://entire.com/gh/entireio/-/trails/2726/changes/git-sync/5|entire.com/gh/entireio/…/5> [nodo <andrea@entire.io>]

> soph <stefan@entire.io>: Main concern: the update can move a ref backward

The new branch takes the commit read after the refusal as the old value, so it overwrites whatever another writer put there without checking which version is newer. The code comment assumes the other writer is usually an older sync. Nothing guarantees that.

• Failure case: this run (A) lists the source with x at S1. A newer run (B) sees x at S2 and its smaller push lands while A's pack is being refused. A reads the target again, finds x at S2, and pushes S2→S1. The target moves back to an older commit and A reports success. That's the same "stale until the next run, reported as success" outcome the PR fixes, just with the order of the two syncs reversed.
• Inconsistent with the update case: in the same function, a planned update whose ref another writer moved to a third commit keeps its original old value. That push fails the compare-and-swap and the run returns an error. So the same concurrent writer is refused for an update and overwritten for a create.
Two alternatives that avoid this:
1. Keep the create in rest with old = zero. The push fails, the run errors, and the next run plans from fresh state. This matches the update case and never moves a ref backward. The cost is one failed run when syncs overlap, which only happens when the lease fails open.
2. Keep the replan, but update the comment and changelog to say a newer run's ref can be moved back until the next run, so that trade-off is a stated choice.
I'd lean toward option 1. If the author keeps the overwrite, a test where the concurrent writer installs a commit after the source's would document the behavior.

Minor:
• Result.Plans and the Pushed count still show the original create, not the update that was actually pushed (syncer.go:1307). The test says so explicitly. It's harmless, but --json output will show a "create" action for what was actually an update.
• The test helper concurrentRefWriter.install runs while holding <http://w.mu|w.mu>. That's fine today, but a future install that calls seen() would deadlock. A one-line comment would cover it.
","pagination_info":"There are no more messages in this thread.
"}

content.text:
Stepping back, here's the problem as I see it now.

**The root problem:** two syncs can write the same target ref at once, because mirror-pipeline's lease fails open. When a run finds a ref changed under it, git-sync can't tell whether the other writer saw an older or a newer source. Whatever it decides inside the run is a guess:

- **Old code:** trust the other writer and drop the ref. Wrong when the other writer is older.
- **This PR:** trust itself and overwrite. Wrong when the other writer is newer, as Soph showed.

**What every other path already does:** it doesn't guess. It sends the push with the old value it planned against. If the ref moved, the target refuses, the run fails with the retryable `ErrTargetRefMoved`, and the next run starts from a fresh read of the source. That holds for:
- the normal replicate path, where a create goes out with old = zero, so a ref someone else created is refused as "already exists";
- the update arm in this same fallback.

The create arm in the fallback is the one place that settles the race itself.

**So the real fix for ENT-3759 is consistency.** The fallback should treat a moved create the way the rest of the code does: skip it only if it's already at the source commit, and otherwise fail with the retryable error. The cost is one failed run when syncs overlap, which only happens when the lease fails open. In exchange, no run reports success over a ref it didn't verify, whichever order the two syncs ran in.

That's Soph's option 1, and it should also make the change smaller than the current one. How mirror-pipeline handles `ErrTargetRefMoved` (how fast it retries) is outside git-sync.

One question to settle first: do you agree the goal is "never claim success over an unverified ref; let the retry resolve it", rather than "converge within the run"?

28:- **Replicate no 
- **Replicate no longer leaves a ref behind when another sync creates it during the batched-create fallback.** After the target refused replicate's pack, the fallback re-read the target and treated every planned create whose ref now existed as done, whatever commit it pointed at. Two syncs of one target can overlap, and an older one could install the ref at the commit it saw while the newer run's pack was being refused; the newer run then reported success with the target behind the source until a later push. A ref already at the source's commit is still treated as done. A ref at any other commit is now pushed as an update from the commit the target holds, so a further concurrent move fails the push instead of being overwritten. ([#135](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/135))

lines: - **`BootstrapLogger` now receives the bootstrap planning and progress lines.** They went only to the `-v` stderr log, so an embedder saw the GitHub size lookup and then nothing until the first checkpoint upload. A bootstrap that stalled while planning logged the size preflight and then nothing until its timeout. Every planning line now also goes to `BootstrapLogger`, with the logger's own attributes and the caller's context. Phase and checkpoint progress goes at Info: planning checkpoints, fetching the commit graph, planned remaining branches with their counts, push attempting, group pushed, branch finalized. A push the target refused or timed out, and resume markers left on the target, go at Warn; a push git-sync stops itself at its byte budget and then splits stays at Info, so a successful bootstrap logs no warnings. Lines logged once per branch (subsumed by trunk, already on target) go at Debug, so a repository with thousands of branches does not emit thousands of Info records per attempt. Error text from the target is sanitized. `-v` shows every line it showed before. ([#134](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/134))

- **Batched bootstrap of a repository with thousands of branches now makes progress.** It used to fetch the commit graph of every branch, one request per branch, before it pushed anything. On a branch-heavy repository that planning alone outlasted a 30-minute sync budget, so each attempt timed out with nothing on the target and started again (ENT-3617). The trunk is now planned and pushed first, so an attempt that times out still leaves it on the target. The remaining branches share one commit-graph fetch. Small branches are pushed in shared packs that create their refs directly, so a fetch and a push deliver many of them. A group whose pack is over budget splits in half. A branch too big to share a pack, or one with a resume marker, keeps its own checkpointed batch as before. `FetchCommitParents` now takes the wants as a list of hashes.

- **Replicate no longer gets stuck after an interrupted bootstrap.** Replicate routes to batched bootstrap only when every desired ref is missing on the target. A bootstrap cut short after the trunk landed left the next run on plain replicate, which sends every missing branch in one pack; a target with a request body limit refused it, and every retry sent the same pack again. When the target refuses replicate's pack for its size or a push deadline, replicate now creates the missing refs with batched bootstrap, planned in one commit-graph fetch against the refs the target already has, then pushes the remaining updates and deletes. Such a run reports relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`.

-- **Replicate no longer leaves a ref behind when another sync creates it during the batched-create fallback.** After the target refused replicate's pack, the fallback re-read the target and treated every planned create whose ref now existed as done, whatever commit it pointed at. Two syncs of one target can overlap, and an older one could install the ref at the commit it saw while the newer run's pack was being refused; the newer run then reported success with the target behind the source until a later push. A ref already at the source's commit is still treated as done. A ref at any other commit is now pushed as an update from the commit the target holds, so a further concurrent move fails the push instead of being overwritten. ([#135](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/135))

+- **Replicate no longer reports success over a ref another sync created during the batched-create fallback.** After the target refused replicate's pack, the fallback re-read the target and treated every planned create whose ref now existed as done, whatever commit it pointed at. Two syncs of one target can overlap, and an older one could install the ref at the commit it saw while the newer run's pack was being refused; the newer run then reported success with the target behind the source until a later push. A ref already at the source's commit is still treated as done. A ref at any other commit is now pushed as the planned create, which the target refuses because the ref exists. The run fails with `ErrTargetRefMoved` (on entire-server; other servers' wording fails the run without that classification), as an update whose ref moved already does, and the next run plans from a fresh listing. The run cannot tell whether the other sync saw an older or a newer source, so it neither keeps nor overwrites that commit. ([#135](https://github.com/entireio/git-sync/pull/135))

- **SSH sources now negotiate protocol v2.** git-sync sent `GIT_PROTOCOL` as a prefix of the remote command, which hosts without a login shell reject (GitHub answers "Invalid command"), so `auto` fell back to v1 on every SSH sync and re-read the full ref advertisement on each RPC. It now sets `GIT_PROTOCOL` in the ssh environment and passes `-o SendEnv=GIT_PROTOCOL`, as git does. A server that does not accept the variable answers v0/v1 and `auto` falls back as before; `--protocol v2` against such a server fails with "source did not negotiate protocol v2". This includes servers that run a login shell but whose sshd does not list `GIT_PROTOCOL` in `AcceptEnv` (stock OpenSSH accepts only `LANG LC_*`): they used to reach v2 through the command prefix and now get v1, as they do with git itself, until `AcceptEnv GIT_PROTOCOL` is added.

- SSH fetches from GitHub intermittently failed with `update object storage: empty packfile`. The SSH transport wrote the request and closed stdin while the server was still streaming its ref advertisement (36 MB for `NixOS/nixpkgs`), and GitHub sometimes dropped a request that arrived that early. The request is now sent only after the advertisement is read, which is what `git` does. On the old code, 2 of 4 runs against `git@github.com:NixOS/nixpkgs.git` failed; with the change, 7 of 7 passed.

- Errors from closing an upload-pack stream (the ssh exit status and the remote's stderr) were dropped in `fetchToStoreV1` and `fetchToStoreV2`, because `CheckClose` wrote to a shadowed `err`. They are now joined into the returned error.

Its target answers a create over an existing ref the way entire-server

## Problem

`replicateBatchedAfterRejection` (added in #132) finishes a replicate run whose single pack the target refused. It re-reads the target's refs and sorts the planned pushes by what the target holds now, but its two arms disagreed about what "already applied" means. The `ActionUpdate` arm treated a ref as applied only when it was at `plan.SourceHash`. The `ActionCreate` arm treated it as applied whenever it was non-zero, so a ref that now existed at **any** hash was dropped from both the batched creates and the follow-up push, and the run returned success.

## Scenario

Two syncs of one target overlap (the caller's per-placement lease fails open by design):

1. Sync A (older, source at H1) and sync B (newer, source at H2) run against the same target.
2. B plans a create for `refs/heads/x` at H2; its pack is refused (body limit or push deadline).
3. A creates `x` at H1 meanwhile.
4. B re-reads the target, sees `x` non-zero, drops it, and reports success with H1 installed.

The mirror is reported ready while it is behind, silently, until some later push event replans H1→H2.

## Fix

A run that finds a planned create already on the target at a different commit cannot tell whether the other sync saw an older source or a newer one. So it neither keeps that commit nor overwrites it. It fails retryably, and the next run plans from a fresh listing.

The create arm now:

- **ref absent** → created by batched bootstrap, as before;
- **ref at the source commit** → skipped, as before;
- **ref at any other commit** → kept as the planned create (old = zero) and sent in the follow-up replicate push with the updates and deletes. The target refuses it because the ref exists. On entire-server the refusal reads "already exists", which `gitproto` classifies as `ErrTargetRefMoved`, so the run fails retryably. The other commands in that push still apply, since git-sync never asks for an atomic push.

This is what the rest of replicate already does when it loses a race:

- the update arm in the same function keeps its planned old hash, so an update whose ref moved to a third commit is refused;
- plain replicate sends a create with old = zero, so a ref someone else created is refused as "already exists".

Against a stock git server the refusal is worded "failed to update ref". It still fails the run, but is not classified as a move. That is the existing, documented limit of `concurrentMoveMarkers`, and it applies to updates as well.

**Why not replan as an update (the first version of this PR):** an update from the commit the target holds overwrites the other sync's commit without knowing which one is newer. If a newer run landed `x` while this run's pack was being refused, this run moved `x` back and reported success. That is the same silent stale target, with the order of the two syncs reversed. Thanks to the review that caught it.

The cost is one failed run when syncs overlap, which only happens when the lease fails open. A run with no concurrent writer behaves as before: after a refused pack, a planned create is either still absent (created) or at the source hash from a push the target applied before giving up (skipped).

## Tests

Two integration tests next to the #132 ones, sharing a fixture. A `receivePackRaw` hook on the test target server stands in for the concurrent sync. It records every command for `refs/heads/x` and, while the first pack (the one the body limit refuses) is being received, writes `x` on the target the way the other sync would.

- `TestRun_IntegrationReplicateRejectedPackCreateMovedConcurrently`: the other sync installs `x` at a commit other than the source's. The target answers a create over an existing ref the way entire-server does ("already exists"). The test asserts that:
  - the run fails with `errors.Is(err, ErrTargetRefMoved)` and relay reason `replicate-pack-rejected`;
  - the batched create of `feature` landed;
  - `x` is left as the other sync wrote it;
  - the retry for `x` was a create (old = zero), not an update.

  On `main` it fails because the run returns nil.
- `TestRun_IntegrationReplicateRejectedPackCreateAppliedConcurrently`: the other sync installs `x` at exactly the source hash. The test asserts that the run succeeds, `x` is at the source hash, and the target received only the refused create, so the ref is skipped rather than re-pushed.

Verified locally on Go 1.27.4:
- `gofmt -s -l .` reports nothing; `go build ./...`, `go vet ./...` and `go test ./...` pass;
- `go test -race ./internal/syncer -run TestRun_IntegrationReplicateRejectedPack` passes;
- `golangci-lint run` (v2.15.0) reports 0 issues.
